tweets.text: $HPE The price is above all the 20/50/100/200 EMAs, with a perfect alignment: 49.93 > 46.12 > 40.51 > 33.99. It has once again reached the top of the sideways range that has been in place for the past two months. If we get a daily close above 55.31, the next targets are 59.11 → 64.09 → 78.60. The fundamentals are telling the same story. Revenue grew 40% last quarter, EPS doubled, the AI backlog reached $5.9 billion, and free cash flow guidance was raised from $2 billion to $3.5 billion. Juniper synergies are also running ahead of schedule. Despite all of this, the stock is trading at just 16x earnings. Morgan Stanley upgraded it to Overweight yesterday, with a $69 price target. If the range breaks out, there’s very little resistance above.

$LLY Q2’26 revenue came in at $23B, up 48% YoY. Mounjaro + Zepbound alone generated $14.9B. Gross margin was 86.3%. Full-year guidance was raised to $85–87B. Foundayo has just entered the market, the Medicare program has opened access to 20 million people at $50/month, and retatrutide is heading to the FDA in Q1 2027. The story is still in its early stages. Technically, the price is above all the 20/50/100/200 EMAs, with the moving averages properly aligned. The channel that started in May remains intact, and MACD has crossed above zero to the upside. If $1,240 breaks, the upside looks wide open. Growth is accelerating, margins are expanding, and there isn’t a single sign of technical deterioration on the chart.

$ASTS – My View After Q2 2026 Earnings This quarter confirmed that ASTS is still in the infrastructure build-out phase. Revenue grew strongly, guidance was maintained, and liquidity improved materially. The main negative is that commercial subscriber revenue is still ahead, so execution remains the key risk. Revenue was $31.5M, roughly double sequentially but below the ~$34–35M expected. Revenue is still coming from gateway equipment and government milestones, meaning direct-to-device monetization is largely a 2027 story. Net loss was $230.9M, mainly due to the ~$125.9M impairment from the BB7 loss. Capex was $610M, reflecting heavy manufacturing and launch spending. The strongest part of the quarter was liquidity. Cash was $2.7B at June 30 and exceeded $3.7B pro forma after the July convertible offering. With limited effective dilution and a low coupon, I view the financing positively. Backlog also increased to $1.3B. The key question now is how quickly cash burn accelerates as deployment scales. On the call, ASTS highlighted 13 satellites in orbit, BB14–16 nearing shipment and production progressing through BB46. The target remains six satellites per month, with roughly 45 satellites expected to support commercial service by early 2027. Beta service is expected to begin with selected operators in 2026. The $1B first-full-commercial-year revenue target remains intact, with potentially up to half coming from government business. Japan’s J-LEO opportunity could also provide up to $1B of non-dilutive capital. The stock fell roughly 4.4% after earnings. To me, this looked more like an expectations-vs-results reaction than a fundamentally bad quarter. Guidance and liquidity remained strong. Bull case: A direct-to-device network connecting to unmodified phones addresses a potentially massive market. The operator model, spectrum, technology and vertical integration could create a strong competitive position. Government business could provide both capital and recurring revenue. Bear case: Execution remains the biggest risk. Launch delays, manufacturing scale-up, network performance, high capex and commercialization timing are all critical. Pricing, subscriber economics and churn are still unproven. What I’m watching: satellite launches, beta performance, government contracts, cash burn, commercial rollout, operator economics and satellite production costs. Bottom line: My long-term thesis has not changed and, if anything, strengthened slightly. The thesis remains: build the constellation, monetize through mobile operators, and use government business to reduce risk. I expect volatility, but I would need to see a meaningful execution failure to materially change my view.

Key reasons: • Strong utility-scale solar market • Resolution of Section 232 uncertainty • Better-calibrated estimates and greater clarity on capital allocation A resolution of the Section 232 issue could restart 2029–2030 bookings, potentially at higher ASPs.

Everyone Is Watching the Robots. I'm Watching the Chips Inside Them. China shipped more than 97% of the world's humanoid robots in the first half of 2026. Global shipments came to about 19,100 units, up from 5,100 a year earlier. AgiBot took 8,400 of them, Unitree 5,900. Tesla, Figure and Agility are nowhere close. That number is impressive. It is also the wrong thing to focus on if you invest in US equities. The robots are being assembled in China. The question that matters for a portfolio is what goes inside them. What is actually in a humanoid A production humanoid contains roughly 1,000 to 2,000 semiconductors, about ten times an industrial robot. Most people assume the AI chip is the story. By volume it is not. The inference processor is the single most expensive line in the bill of materials, but only 1-3% of the device count. The other 97-99% is analog and mixed-signal: motor drive transistors, gate drivers, position encoders, current-sense amplifiers, battery monitors, power regulators, IMUs, force-sensing chains. A humanoid has 40+ joint drives and 225-470 sensor devices. Every one needs conditioning and control. So there are two very different businesses here. The brain.NVIDIA's Jetson Thor is the reference platform: Blackwell GPU, 128GB of LPDDR5X at 273GB/s, 2,070 FP4 TFLOPS inside a 130-watt envelope. Production modules run $2,999 in 1,000-unit lots. Qualcomm launched Dragonwing IQ10 at CES 2026 for full-size humanoids. Both American. The body.Texas Instruments and Analog Devices sit in dominant positions across multiple layers of the stack. Infineon, STMicroelectronics, onsemi, NXP, Microchip and Renesas fill the rest. Renesas now publishes a complete humanoid reference design: nine-axis motor control, body controller, vision, battery management, all in one configuration. On memory, this is where I see people get it wrong. Humanoids do not use HBM. They use LPDDR5X plus NAND storage. Micron's CEO says a humanoid carries about ten times the memory of an average L2+ vehicle. Directionally right, but run the numbers. 500,000 robots in 2030 at 128GB each is 64 petabytes of DRAM. Even at 1TB per robot it is half an exabyte, against an industry shipping hundreds. Robots are not the memory cycle. They are an option on the back end of it. The numbers nobody quotes Silicon content per humanoid is $1,400-3,000, depending on whether you take UBS or Morgan Stanley. Multiply by 19,100 units and the entire global humanoid chip market in the first half of 2026 was $27-57 million. NVIDIA's fiscal 2026 revenue was $215.9 billion. The forecasts run wide. Smart Analytics Global sees 60,000 units this year and 500,000 by 2030, producing around $3 billion of robot revenue. Morgan Stanley models a $5 trillion market by 2050, with robotics semiconductor demand rising from $2.2 billion in 2025 to $1.8 trillion. UBS puts that same 2050 chip TAM at $177 billion. A tenfold gap between two banks tells you these are assumptions, not forecasts. How this shows up in earnings It doesn't, yet. No large chipmaker reports humanoid revenue separately because there is nothing to report. NVIDIA's robotics business was around 1% of sales, and from fiscal 2027 it is folded into a combined Edge Computing segment. TI, ADI and Infineon book it inside industrial. This is a design-win cycle, not a revenue cycle. The harvest is 2029-2032. The risk nobody prices If 97% of robots are Chinese, the chip decision is Chinese too. AgiBot is working with domestic AI chip firms. Huawei is supplying Ascend and Kunpeng to UBTech. Rockchip's RK3588 already ships in several Chinese humanoids. Meanwhile the FCC has added Chinese humanoids to its covered list, blocking new authorizations. The brain layer is the most exposed, because that is exactly what China is trying to replace. The analog and control layer is harder to copy and harder to displace. That is where I would rather own the exposure.
